title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (FIGO PALM-COEIN)
summary: Structured FIGO PALM-COEIN classification standardizes workup of abnormal uterine bleeding and guides a stepwise medical-to-surgical management approach.
key_points: PALM = structural causes: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia
COEIN = nonstructural causes: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not-yet-classified
Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by impact on quality of life, not a fixed blood-loss volume
First-line workup: pregnancy test, CBC, TSH, coagulation studies if indicated, pelvic ultrasound
Endometrial sampling for age 45+ or younger with risk factors (obesity, PCOS, unopposed estrogen, persistent bleeding)
Saline sonohysterography or hysteroscopy used when focal lesion (polyp/fibroid) is suspected
Leiomyomas subclassified FIGO 0-8 by relation to endometrial cavity and uterine serosa
management: Medical first-line: combined hormonal contraceptives, cyclic/continuous progestins, or levonorgestrel IUD
Tranexamic acid or NSAIDs for ovulatory heavy bleeding when contraception isn't needed/desired
GnRH agonist/antagonist (± add-back therapy) for fibroid-related bleeding, short-term or preoperatively
Hysteroscopic polypectomy or myomectomy for cavity-distorting lesions
Endometrial ablation for refractory bleeding when fertility is no longer desired
Uterine artery embolization as a uterus-sparing option for symptomatic fibroids
Hysterectomy is definitive for refractory bleeding or when malignancy is present

title: Ectopic Pregnancy
summary: Early risk stratification and hCG/ultrasound criteria distinguish candidates for methotrexate therapy from those needing surgical management of ectopic pregnancy.
key_points: Risk factors: prior ectopic, tubal surgery/damage, PID/salpingitis, IUD in place at conception, smoking, ART
Classic triad (pain, bleeding, amenorrhea) is often incomplete at presentation
Discriminatory hCG zone ~3,500 mIU/mL: an intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on TVUS above this
Normal early viable IUP hCG rises at least ~35% over 48 hours; slower rise suggests ectopic/nonviable pregnancy
Methotrexate candidacy: hemodynamically stable, hCG generally <5,000, mass ≤3.5-4 cm, no fetal cardiac activity
Methotrexate requires normal renal/hepatic/marrow function and reliable follow-up
Absolute contraindications to methotrexate: rupture, instability, breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, significant renal/hepatic disease
management: Confirm diagnosis with serial hCG trends plus transvaginal ultrasound; exclude heterotopic pregnancy after ART
Single-dose IM methotrexate with hCG checks on days 4 and 7, expecting ≥15% decline
Repeat dosing or convert to surgery if hCG decline is inadequate
Surgery (salpingostomy or salpingectomy) for rupture, instability, or methotrexate failure/contraindication
Salpingectomy favored over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is healthy
Give Rh immune globulin if the patient is Rh-negative
Counsel on recurrence risk and need for early ultrasound in future pregnancies
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193, Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy (2018; verify current reaffirmation status at acog.org)
ACOG Practice Bulletin, Early Pregnancy Loss (current edition — verify at acog.org)

title: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease and Common STIs
summary: Low-threshold clinical diagnosis and CDC-directed empiric antibiotic regimens for PID and common STIs, paired with age-based screening recommendations.
key_points: PID minimum criteria: cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness in a sexually active woman with pelvic pain
Supportive criteria: oral temp >101°F, abnormal discharge, elevated ESR/CRP, documented gonorrhea/chlamydia
Low specificity of criteria plus high cost of missed diagnosis support a low threshold to treat empirically
Chlamydia and gonorrhea are diagnosed by NAAT on vaginal/cervical swab or urine
Screen all sexually active women under 25 annually for chlamydia/gonorrhea; screen older women with risk factors
Test every PID patient for gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, and syphilis; consider M. genitalium
Hospitalize for PID if pregnant, failing oral therapy, tubo-ovarian abscess, or surgical emergency can't be excluded
management: Outpatient PID: ceftriaxone IM once, plus doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg PO twice daily, both for 14 days
Inpatient/parenteral PID: cefotetan or cefoxitin plus doxycycline, or clindamycin plus gentamicin, step down to oral once improving
Uncomplicated chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days (azithromycin single dose as an alternative)
Uncomplicated gonorrhea: single weight-based IM ceftriaxone dose; treat chlamydia presumptively if not excluded
Evaluate and presumptively treat sex partners from the prior 60 days for gonorrhea/chlamydia
Advise abstinence until therapy is complete and partners are treated; retest for reinfection at 3 months
Drain a tubo-ovarian abscess (surgically or image-guided) if it fails to respond to antibiotics

title: Contraception (CDC MEC and Method Selection)
summary: CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria categories match contraceptive methods to patient comorbidities, alongside effectiveness tiers and method-specific safety flags.
key_points: US MEC categories: 1 no restriction, 2 benefits outweigh risks, 3 risks usually outweigh benefits, 4 unacceptable risk
Tier 1 effectiveness (<1 pregnancy/100 woman-years): implant, hormonal and copper IUDs, sterilization
Tier 2 effectiveness (typical-use failure roughly mid-single to low-double digits per 100 woman-years): injectable, pill, patch, ring
Tier 3 effectiveness (least effective typical use): barrier methods, fertility awareness, withdrawal
Combined hormonal methods are MEC 4 in smokers 35+ (heavy use), migraine with aura, VTE/thrombophilia history
IUDs (copper or levonorgestrel) are safe (MEC 1-2) in most comorbidities and serve as top emergency contraception options
Progestin-only methods are MEC 1-2 across most cardiovascular risk factors, including much VTE history
management: Assess reproductive goals and comorbidities, then apply the MEC category before recommending a method
Offer long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) first-line given superior effectiveness and continuation rates
Avoid estrogen-containing methods in MEC 3/4 conditions (aura migraine, heavy smoking 35+, VTE/thrombophilia)
Use the companion Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR) for initiation timing and side-effect management
Counsel on emergency contraception: copper IUD is most effective; levonorgestrel or ulipristal oral options otherwise
Reassess MEC eligibility whenever a new diagnosis (hypertension, VTE, aura migraine) arises
Recommend dual method use with barriers for STI protection regardless of primary contraceptive chosen
citations: CDC U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024, MMWR Recommendations and Reports Vol. 73, No. RR-4
CDC U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024 (verify at cdc.gov)

title: Cervical Cancer Screening and Abnormal Result Management
summary: Age- and history-based screening intervals combine with ASCCP risk-based thresholds to decide when abnormal cytology or HPV results warrant colposcopy versus treatment.
key_points: Screening start age and primary modality vary by guideline body (age 21 vs. 25, cytology vs. primary HPV) — verify current source
Ages 21-29: cytology alone roughly every 3 years is the common baseline recommendation
Ages 30-65: preferred strategies are primary HPV testing or HPV/cytology co-testing roughly every 5 years, or cytology alone every 3 years
Screening may stop after age 65 with adequate negative screening history and no CIN2+ in the past 25 years
ASCCP risk-based management sets the colposcopy referral threshold at roughly 4% immediate CIN3+ risk
Very high immediate CIN3+ risk (roughly 60%+) supports proceeding directly to treatment without confirmatory colposcopy
Management depends on current result plus prior screening/biopsy history, not the current result alone
management: Triage abnormal cytology (ASC-US or worse) or a positive primary HPV test using current risk-based action thresholds
Refer to colposcopy once estimated CIN3+ risk meets or exceeds the guideline threshold
Consider expedited treatment without colposcopy when risk is very high (e.g., HPV16/18-positive with high-grade cytology)
Use extended HPV genotyping (16/18 or other high-risk types) to refine the risk estimate for triage
Intensify post-colposcopy/post-treatment surveillance (more frequent HPV testing) rather than resuming the routine interval
Continue surveillance for at least 25 years after treatment for CIN2+, even past age 65
Maintain longitudinal screening/biopsy history, since management depends on it as well as the current test
citations: ASCCP Risk-Based Management Consensus Guidelines for Abnormal Cervical Cancer Screening Tests and Cancer Precursors, 2019 (verify current update at asccp.org)
American Cancer Society Cervical Cancer Screening Guideline, 2020 Update
ACOG Practice Advisory, Cervical Cancer Screening and Risk-Based Management (current edition — verify at acog.org)
